newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Credit Suisse sees SNB keeping policy easy.
newsitem.headline: Credit Suisse sees SNB keeping policy easy.

text.p: Credit Suisse said it expected the Swiss National Bank (SNB) to maintain its generous monetary policy until there were clearer signs of an economic upturn and that the Swiss franc would remain steady over the next year.

"As long as there are no clearer indications of an economic recovery, interest rates will remain low for the time being and the supply of money will remain generous," analyst Thomas Steinemann wrote in an economic research report.

Citing economic stagnation and practically no inflation danger, he said money supply would again in 1997 grow above the SNB's medium-term annual target of one percent, but that the pace of growth would slow.
Adjusted central bank money supply grew 5.0 percent in 1996 compared with the fourth quarter of 1995. Gross domestic product fell 0.7 percent in 1996, but fourth-quarter GDP was flat.

"But a discount rate cut is still not an issue," he added, saying such a step was conceivable only if the Swiss franc gained strongly, for example if a broad economic and monetary union sparked flight into the franc as a safe haven currency.
The 100-point spread between the 1.0 percent discount rate and money market rates was also wide, he said, adding market rates had to sink to around 1.2 percent for the SNB to cut.

On a trade-weighted basis, the Swiss franc had fallen 11 percent in the year to February due to the SNB's expansive policy, differentials with dollar interest rates, and the franc's abdication of its safe haven role ahead of EMU, he said.

"The creation of a hard-currency EMU is already widely discounted, so the franc may not face great upward pressure. Only a broad currency union including southern European countries would drive the franc to its old highs," he said.
"We thus expect the franc to firm only slightly over a one-year horizon to between 84 and 86 francs per 100 marks."
